metadata.title: Is Registering a Subsidiary the Same as Staying Compliant?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether registering a subsidiary finishes the compliance job or starts a recurring one. Lands the carry-out that a registered entity is compliant one deadline at a time, for as long as it exists.

beats.narration_text: Someone on a legal team registers a subsidiary and figures that's the end of it. Wrong last word. Registered is a moment. Current is a status. Liam, take them through the difference.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'We registered the subsidiary. Are we done?', hesitates on 'done', corrects to 'current', lands the real question

props.text:

the subsidiary.

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('done' -> 'current') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's what a certificate of incorporation actually is. The state ticked a box that this entity existed the day it was filed. Nothing more. The state never signed up to watch it forever, and it doesn't. When a required filing goes unmet, good standing drops on the state's clock — no notice sent, no human at the state deciding, nobody asking permission. They optimized incorporation for making entities cheap to create; the cost is that keeping one alive is entirely the owner's problem, and the state's default is to notice nothing.

shot.new_visual_element: A sealed certificate card, filed and stamped once; a 'NOT IN GOOD STANDING' stamp landing on it later with no hand, no decision, no arrow from anyone

production_viz.label: A certificate is a snapshot, not a status
production_viz.mechanic: A certificate card fades in, stamped 'FILED' once, and sits still. Time passes (a faint calendar line ticks beneath it). Without any hand or arrow entering the frame, a second stamp -- 'NOT IN GOOD STANDING' -- lands on the card on its own. A caption fades in beneath: 'nobody asked permission.'

beats.narration_text: Every entity you register carries its own recurring calendar. Four fields. An annual or biennial report, due on its own date. A registered agent — a real person or service at a real address in that state — who has to stay current. A foreign-qualification filing in every other state where the entity does business. And, in some states, a franchise tax on its own schedule. Uniform shape per entity, tracked separately per entity — the shape is simple, but the count scales. One entity operating in three states is three calendars, not one. Watch the anchor: a Delaware subsidiary spun up three years ago for a single product launch. Nobody has checked its filing date since.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- four field chips lighting in turn (report date / registered agent / foreign qualification / franchise tax), then a dim, unlabeled entity card set off to the side

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- four recurring dates, then the unwatched subsidiary
production_viz.mechanic: Four chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a recurring obligation (report date / registered agent / foreign qualification / franchise tax), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A single card appears off to the side, dim and outlined only, reading 'DE subsidiary -- product launch' with no dates filled in -- visibly incomplete against the four-field shape just shown. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS, FILLED IN, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: That unwatched report date comes and goes. The subsidiary quietly slides into 'not in good standing' — and nobody at the company notices, because nobody was watching. It only surfaces later, when a financing round's diligence team pulls a status certificate and finds the entity delinquent. Two directions this generalizes. Current at home is not compliant everywhere: a foreign qualification is its own separate deadline in its own state, and standing in Delaware says nothing about your registration in California. Clean today is not clean forever: the next filing date is already on the calendar, for every entity on the list. They optimized this system for uniformity — same four-field shape in every state, for every entity — at the expense of any warning system. There is none. Compliance runs on a schedule you have to keep yourself.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the dim card lighting up with its filing history and flagged delinquent; then split into 'current at home is not compliant everywhere' and 'clean today is not clean forever'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- found lapsed in diligence
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 DIM CARD RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in one field at a time (report date / registered agent / foreign qualification) until a fourth field lights terracotta: 'status: DELINQUENT'. It splits into two cards: left reads 'home state: current' with a struck-through 'COMPLIANT EVERYWHERE' beneath it labelled 'current at home is not compliant everywhere'; right reads 'list: clean today' with a faint new date appearing at its edge labelled 'clean today is not clean forever'.

beats.narration_text: A registered entity isn't compliant forever — it's compliant one deadline at a time, for as long as it exists.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm on a legal team and I want a first-pass entity-compliance calendar. List every kind of legal entity a mid-sized company might have — parent, domestic subsidiaries, foreign qualifications, single-purpose LLCs, everything. For each one, give me four fields: home state, next annual or biennial report deadline, registered-agent status, and any foreign qualifications with their own deadlines. Then flag the two most likely to have already slipped into 'not in good standing' because nobody was watching. Go deeper: take a Delaware subsidiary spun up three years ago for a one-off product launch — walk me through exactly what to check today to know whether it's still current.
